tagline.text: Come face to face in the forest with the Philippine eagle, the national bird and one of the world's largest

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (January–April, with less rain, is most pleasant)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–3,000 per person (per day, starting from downtown Davao)

image.credit: shankar s. / CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A conservation and breeding facility run by the Philippine Eagle Foundation, about an hour northwest of downtown Davao in the forest of Malagos. See the endangered national bird up close, and learn the story of the world's first successful captive breeding in 1992, along with the conservation work protecting the forest.
The Philippine eagle is one of the largest eagles in the world, measuring about
in body length with a wingspan of about
2m
. It's known for its shaggy crest of head feathers, a large bluish-tinged bill, and sharp blue-gray eyes, and lives only in the forests of the Philippines. It was named the national bird in
, but with forests disappearing, only a few hundred pairs are estimated to remain in the wild, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies it as "Critically Endangered."

The Philippine Eagle Center is run by the Philippine Eagle Foundation, a nonprofit working to protect this bird, and sits in the forest of Malagos, Baguio District, Davao City. The foundation's roots trace back to a "monkey-eating eagle" conservation program begun in
; the bird's name changed to today's "Philippine eagle" in the late 1970s, and the program relaunched as a private foundation in
. The center treats eagles rescued while injured, shelters individuals unable to return to the wild, and continues breeding research.
What put this place on the map worldwide was Pag-asa ("hope"), a male eagle born at the center on
January 15, 1992

. Born through artificial insemination and incubation after 14 years of research, he was the world's first captive-bred Philippine eagle, and the center has since succeeded in breeding dozens of times. Pag-asa himself became a father in
, and remained a symbol of Philippine eagle conservation until he passed away at age 28 in
. Because Philippine eagles typically lay just one egg every two years, every single successful breeding is extremely precious.

The visitor trail follows a forest path shaded by tall trees and ferns, passing large enclosures along the way where you'll meet the Philippine eagle along with various birds of prey and native animals. This is less a flashy zoo with shows and rides than a conservation education facility, a place to walk quietly, read the information panels, and observe the birds. See the Davao City entry for touring downtown; this place is especially recommended for family trips with children, travelers who love birds and nature, and anyone interested in the story of the Philippines' endangered species.

blocks.title: Seeing the Philippine eagle up close

children.text: In spacious, forest-like enclosures, you can watch Philippine eagles perched on branches, surveying their surroundings. Each bird has a sign with its name and its rescue or breeding story, making it fun to read about one after another.
An exhibit introducing the birth and life of Pag-asa, the world's first successfully captive-bred eagle, shows just how long the research journey was to raise a single bird.
Opened in
, this memorial features a sculpture honoring Geothermica, an eagle that died while on conservation loan to Singapore. It tells the story of Philippine eagle diplomacy and international cooperation.
The whole trail runs beneath dense forest shade, keeping it relatively cool even at midday. It's a good place for a slow walk, enjoying the orchids and ferns clinging to the trees and the birdsong.

blocks.title: Other birds of prey and native animals

children.text: You can also see other raptors such as the Brahminy kite, along with native animals like the Philippine warty pig and long-tailed macaque. Which animals are on display varies depending on rescue and treatment cases.
With advance booking, a guide will explain the eagles' ecology, the threats they face, and the foundation's forest-ranger and nest-monitoring work. It's especially worthwhile with kids.

The foundation funds its operations through an adoption program that sponsors the care and feeding costs of individual eagles, along with souvenir sales. Even a single souvenir contributes to conservation work.

Malagos Garden Resort is a separate facility with its own entrance fee and show times. Combining both places is more time-efficient if you charter a vehicle for the day.

1 hour 10 minutes
from Cebu, with one-way fares around

1 hour 10 minutes–1 hour 40 minutes
by car, so rather than going straight there on arrival day, it's more relaxed to stay overnight downtown and head out the next morning.

Tell the driver "Philippine Eagle Center, Malagos" and they'll drop you at the turnoff. Departure terminals change routes often, so it's best to check with your accommodation.
Travel agencies and hotels downtown sell half-day and full-day tours combining the eagle center and Malagos Garden Resort. Including transport and entrance fees, these run about
per person, more economical than a private charter for a small group.
Davao sits outside the typhoon path and gets fairly even rain year-round with no clearly defined dry or wet season, so the center is good to visit any time of year. Still,
January–April
has relatively less rain and pleasant trail conditions, while
June–October
brings frequent afternoon showers. Being in a forest at the foot of the mountains, it's a bit cooler than downtown, with daytime temperatures running around
The birds are most active in the cool morning, and often rest in the shade by midday. Going right after opening,
, gives you a better chance of seeing active eagles and fewer group tours. Weekends, school breaks, and
August
, when Davao's biggest festival, Kadayawan, is held, can get crowded with families and school groups.

The center itself has no lodging, so most visitors stay downtown in Davao and come for half a day. See the Davao City entry for detailed downtown accommodation and dining information. If you'd like a night in the quiet forest, Malagos Garden Resort right next door offers rooms, with gardens and butterfly and bird viewing facilities that make it popular with families with kids. Rates run about
a night depending on room type.

There aren't many restaurants around the center, so get simple snacks and drinks at the shop, and a proper meal at the Malagos Garden Resort restaurant or restaurants around the Calinan market. The Calinan and Baguio District area is Davao's orchard belt, where you can buy seasonal fruits like durian, mangosteen, rambutan, and marang cheaply from roadside stalls, with the season running roughly
August–October
. The Malagos area is also known for handmade chocolate made from Davao-grown cacao, a great souvenir.
Operating hours, closed days, and fees can change based on the foundation's circumstances. Check the foundation's official channels before you visit, and book group visits or guided tours in advance.
The eagles in the enclosures are a bit of a distance away, so a telephoto lens or binoculars let you see even their expressions in detail.
For photos through the wire mesh, hold your lens close to the wire and focus on the bird, and the mesh will blur out of a clean shot. Don't use flash.
The forest trail can be slippery after rain, so wear comfortable sneakers and bring mosquito repellent.
Ticket sales and the gift shop are easiest with cash. It helps to bring small bills.

If combining this with downtown Davao sightseeing in one day, the center in the morning and downtown in the afternoon works well. Eden Nature Park is in a different direction, so splitting it onto another day is more relaxed.
Foreign visitors can also join the foundation's eagle adoption program, and sponsoring a specific eagle with your child and getting updates on it can make for a great memory.

Before anything else, this center is a conservation facility caring for an endangered species. Banging on cages, shouting, feeding the birds, and using flash photography all cause severe stress to the birds and must never be done.
Don't put fingers or objects through the wire mesh. Birds of prey have extremely powerful beaks and talons.
Flying drones or holding a selfie stick close to the enclosures may be prohibited or stopped by staff, so follow their guidance.

Davao City has relatively good security by Philippine standards, but travel advisories are in effect for some parts of Mindanao. It's best to check your home country's regional advisory levels before you go.
Public transport back thins out in the late afternoon. If you came by public transport, it's safest to leave the center before 3 PM.

Capturing or killing a Philippine eagle carries severe legal penalties. If you find an injured eagle in the wild, report it to the foundation or the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).
Mindanao's largest city, about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
from the center by car, known for its fruit market, seafood, and clean streets.
A garden-style resort right next to the center, offering bird shows, a butterfly garden, and Davao-grown cacao chocolate.
A highland retreat on the southwestern slopes of Davao, about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
from the center by car. Its cool pine forest and the Skyrider zipline are popular.
The Philippines' highest peak and home to wild Philippine eagles, letting you walk through the very forest home of the eagles you saw at the center.
A beach-resort island about
15 minutes
from the downtown Davao pier by boat, a good place to relax by the sea the day after visiting the forest.
